stories.title: Five months treating bugs like patients and coding agents like a medical team
stories.blurb: CockroachLabs ran a 5-month experiment treating their codebase like a hospital — bugs are patients, coding agents are the medical team. It's one of the most concrete, honest post-mortems on agentic AI workflows in production you'll find. Required reading if you're using Claude Code or any AI coding assistant at scale.

stories.title: Mxc: Microsoft Execution Containers version 1.0.0
stories.blurb: Microsoft ships v1.0 of Execution Containers — policy-driven sandboxing specifically designed for AI agents running on Windows. As Claude Code and similar tools get more autonomous, containment becomes essential. This is Microsoft's answer to the 'what happens when the agent does something bad' problem.

stories.title: Nix wrote half of my debugger
stories.blurb: A fascinating deep-dive into how Nix's reproducibility guarantees let the author offload entire swaths of debugger infrastructure to the package manager. If you've been skeptical of Nix's complexity-to-payoff ratio, this is a compelling argument for the payoff side. Nix as a force multiplier for tooling.

stories.title: LineageOS 24.0
stories.blurb: LineageOS 24.0 lands with Android 15 support, bringing de-Googled Android to a fresh wave of devices. The gold standard for privacy-conscious mobile users who want control over their hardware. If you've been waiting to flash your device, now's the time to check the supported list.

stories.title: Nitter: Update Oct 10th seeking funding and legal help
stories.blurb: Nitter — the privacy-first Twitter/X frontend — is fighting for survival, now publicly seeking funding and legal support. X's legal pressure on scraping-adjacent projects is intensifying, and Nitter is the canary in the coal mine for open-access to public social data. Worth paying attention to.

stories.title: 2D Vehicles
stories.blurb: Top-scored post of the batch: a delightful browser-based physics playground where you build and drive 2D vehicles. Pure creative coding joy — the kind of project that reminds you why people fell in love with the web. Poke around the source if you want ideas for your own physics simulations.

stories.title: The Lightbulb Computer
stories.blurb: A computer built entirely from lightbulbs — no transistors, no ICs. This is computing fundamentals made viscerally visible, and the interactive explanations are some of the best hardware pedagogy on the web. Mesmerizing to watch logic gates glow.

stories.title: A city-building game in which the city would prefer you didn't
stories.blurb: A browser city-builder that satirizes zoning laws, NIMBYism, and bureaucratic obstruction — the city's systems actively fight your attempts to build housing. It's clever game design as political commentary, and it's genuinely fun. Playable right now in your browser.

stories.title: Build your own decision model
stories.blurb: A practical framework for building personal decision models — structured thinking you can actually code up and use. Pairs surprisingly well with AI-assisted workflows where you want the LLM to reason within your constraints rather than its own. Immediately actionable for any developer making architectural or product decisions.

stories.title: I paid people to try and follow my README
stories.blurb: The author paid strangers to follow their project's README and documented every stumble — a real usability study on documentation. The results are humbling and the lessons are immediately actionable. If you ship open-source code, this will make you rethink every assumption you've baked into your docs.

stories.title: Grieving the loss of details
stories.blurb: A thoughtful, widely-discussed essay on how modern computing abstractions strip away details that used to be visible and meaningful — and what we lose as a result. 382 comments means this hit a nerve. Essential reading for anyone who thinks carefully about software craft.

stories.title: Show HN: BetterWispr – Free, open-source dictation for Mac
stories.blurb: A free, open-source dictation app for Mac that competes with Wispr Flow — system-wide voice-to-text without a subscription. Low HN score but extremely relevant for the macOS power user. If you've been eyeing Whisper-powered dictation tools, this one's worth trying today.

stories.title: OpenSCAD the Programmers Solid 3D CAD Modeller
stories.blurb: OpenSCAD resurfaces on HN and reminds us why code-first 3D modeling is underrated — you describe geometry in a scripting language, no mouse-pushing required. If you can write TypeScript, you can design printable parts. 132 comments full of tips and project showcases.

stories.title: Chernobyl particles reveal unexpectedly stable nuclear fuel after 40 years
stories.blurb: New analysis of radioactive particles ejected from Chernobyl shows the nuclear fuel has remained far more chemically stable than models predicted over 40 years. This upends assumptions in nuclear waste containment science. Genuinely surprising result with long-term policy implications.

stories.title: Food processing influences metabolism and brain activity
stories.blurb: Virginia Tech researchers show that ultra-processed foods don't just affect the gut — they measurably alter brain activity and metabolic signaling via the hormone hutelin. The mechanism is clearer than 'junk food is bad' and adds real neuroscience to the ultra-processed food debate.

stories.title: The tilde in your PATH may not be your HOME
stories.blurb: A sharp little security/correctness gotcha: `~` in PATH doesn't always expand to $HOME, and the cases where it doesn't can silently break things or create privilege-escalation vectors. The kind of shell knowledge that saves you from a weird 2am incident. Actionable and immediately applicable.

stories.title: Show HN: Diffle, a keyboard-centric diff viewer with LSP support
stories.blurb: Diffle is a terminal diff viewer built for keyboard-first developers, with LSP support baked in so you get syntax-aware diffs. If you live in the CLI and have been frustrated by clunky diff tooling, this is worth a look today. Clean project, actively developed.

stories.title: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
stories.blurb: Published in Nature: a method for retrofitting existing LLMs to process raw bytes instead of tokens, bypassing tokenization entirely. This has big implications for code models, multilingual support, and robustness to adversarial inputs. Foundational research that will ripple through AI tooling.

stories.title: Getting old Macromedia Director Games to run on modern Hardware
stories.blurb: A deep forensic dive into cracking Macromedia Director's 1990s copy protection to revive classic CD-ROM games on modern hardware. Superb reverse engineering writeup with layers of DRM archaeology. If you love the intersection of software history and low-level sleuthing, this is a treat.

stories.title: How big is a Git commit?
stories.blurb: A concise, well-illustrated breakdown of exactly what data a Git commit object contains and how Git calculates its size. The kind of foundational knowledge that makes you a better developer and helps you reason about repo performance. Short, sharp, bookmark-worthy.
